source_refs.quote: Call me Ishmael.
I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world.

interpretations.detail: Ishmael is a weathered man in his early thirties wearing a charcoal greatcoat.

source_refs.quote: Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses,

interpretations.detail: The visual combines the drizzly mood and coffin-warehouse image stated by Ishmael.

source_refs.quote: then, I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I can. This is my substitute for pistol and ball.
I quietly take to the ship.

interpretations.detail: His posture becoming steadier visualizes the sea as a remedy without adding an event.

source_refs.quote: There now is your insular city of the Manhattoes, belted round by wharves as Indian isles by coral reefs—commerce surrounds it with her surf. Right and left, the streets take you waterward.

interpretations.detail: Manhattan, its wharves, commerce, and waterward streets are directly described.

source_refs.quote: What do you see?—Posted like silent sentinels all around the town, stand thousands upon thousands of mortal men fixed in ocean reveries.

interpretations.detail: The locations, Sabbath mood, crowds, and sentinel comparison come from the paragraph.

source_refs.quote: But these are all landsmen; of week days pent up in lath and plaster—tied to counters, nailed to benches, clinched to desks. How then is this? Are the green fields gone? What do they here?

interpretations.detail: The men leaving workspaces for the pier joins details stated in the same paragraph.

source_refs.quote: But look! here come more crowds, pacing straight for the water, and seemingly bound for a dive. Strange! Nothing will content them but the extremest limit of the land;

interpretations.detail: The crowd and its movement toward the furthest edge of land are explicit.

source_refs.quote: Inlanders all, they come from lanes and alleys, streets and avenues—north, east, south, and west. Yet here they all unite.

interpretations.detail: Compass and rigging foreground the paragraph's metaphor without making magnetism literal.

source_refs.quote: Take almost any path you please, and ten to one it carries you down in a dale, and leaves you there by a pool in the stream. There is magic in it.

interpretations.detail: The high country, path, dale, pool, and stream are directly described.

source_refs.quote: Yes, as every one knows, meditation and water are wedded for ever.
What is the chief element he employs?

interpretations.detail: The traveler watching his reflection gives a visual bridge between meditation and landscape painting.

source_refs.quote: yet all were vain, unless the shepherd’s eye were fixed upon the magic stream before him.

interpretations.detail: The landscape elements and the shepherd's focus on the stream are drawn from the passage.

source_refs.quote: what is the one charm wanting?—Water—there is not a drop of water there! Were Niagara but a cataract of sand, would you travel your thousand miles to see it?

interpretations.detail: Prairie flowers and the hypothetical sand cataract both come directly from the passage.

source_refs.quote: But that same image, we ourselves see in all rivers and oceans. It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all.

interpretations.detail: Narcissus and the reflection as life's ungraspable phantom are stated in the source.

source_refs.quote: For to go as a passenger you must needs have a purse, and a purse is but a rag unless you have something in it.

interpretations.detail: Contrasting paying passengers with Ishmael's chosen working deck visualizes his stated distinction.

source_refs.quote: No, when I go to sea, I go as a simple sailor, right before the mast, plumb down into the forecastle, aloft there to the royal mast-head.

interpretations.detail: Ishmael's rank, location, orders, and movement among the spars are directly described.

source_refs.quote: What of it, if some old hunks of a sea-captain orders me to get a broom and sweep down the decks?
Who ain’t a slave? Tell me that.

interpretations.detail: Sweeping under a captain's order is the example Ishmael gives.

source_refs.quote: Again, I always go to sea as a sailor, because they make a point of paying me for my trouble, whereas they never pay passengers a single penny that I ever heard of.

interpretations.detail: Coins visualize the source's contrast between sailors being paid and passengers paying.

source_refs.quote: Finally, I always go to sea as a sailor, because of the wholesome exercise and pure air of the fore-castle deck.

interpretations.detail: Exercise, pure forecastle air, and headwinds are stated directly.

source_refs.quote: this the invisible police officer of the Fates, who has the constant surveillance of me, and secretly dogs me,

interpretations.detail: Rigging shadows suggest fate while avoiding a literal new character.

source_refs.quote: Chief among these motives was the overwhelming idea of the great whale himself. Such a portentous and mysterious monster roused all my curiosity.

interpretations.detail: The whale, its mystery, distant seas, island bulk, and danger are directly described.

source_refs.quote: as for me, I am tormented with an everlasting itch for things remote. I love to sail forbidden seas, and land on barbarous coasts.

interpretations.detail: The departure visualizes Ishmael's stated attraction to remote seas and coasts.

source_refs.quote: the great flood-gates of the wonder-world swung open,
one grand hooded phantom, like a snow hill in the air.

interpretations.detail: The whale procession and hooded snow-hill phantom are the chapter's closing vision.
